spec.title: The padlock is a lie until you read the cert
spec.intro:
An auditor asks one two-part question — "is the data encrypted at rest AND in transit?" — and a
green padlock is offered as the answer. It is not the answer. You are handed real cryptographic
artifacts and asked to read each half's truth directly off the bytes: sort hash from encrypt from
encode by running the real transform, peel the real www.google.com certificate to the one field
that anchors the in-transit claim, assemble the TLS 1.3 handshake until the sim refuses an illegal
move with the real RFC 8446 alert, and click the single field that breaks each broken cert.

Every value you reveal is the real parser / state-machine / transform over the real artifact — the
same fields `openssl x509 -text` prints, the same return codes `openssl verify` emits (0/10/18/62),
and SHA-256("") = e3b0c442… recomputed live. Nothing is invented; the transform is the answer key.
Start on the "Sort · SHA-256" card.

tasks.instruction:
On the "Sort · SHA-256('hello')" card, sort it into ONE-WAY HASH and label it HASH. Click
"prove it" — the engine recomputes SHA-256 and never recovers "hello", so this card is a
one-way hash, not an encoding. Read the digest the transform produced.

hints.nudge: Which of the three can you NEVER turn back, with any key? That pile is the one-way hash.

hints.concept: §4.1 — hashing is one-way (no key); if 'prove it' can't recover the input it is HASH

hints.reveal: Label the SHA-256 card HASH; the transform produced 2cf24dba… and never reverses

tasks.explain:
The class is DERIVED by running the real transform, not read off an answer key — SHA-256 is
one-way, so the engine can recompute the digest but never recover "hello". "It looks scrambled"
is not "it is protected": a hash protects integrity, not confidentiality.

tasks.instruction:
Take the "Sort · base64('hello')" card, sort it into ENCODE, and label it ENCODE. Click
"prove it" — base64-decoding it recovers "hello" with NO key. Read the encoded value the
transform produced (aGVsbG8=).

hints.nudge: Which one turns back into the original with NO secret at all? That is the encode pile.

hints.concept: §4.1 — encoding is reversible with NO key (RFC 4648); base64 hides nothing

hints.reveal: Label the base64 card ENCODE; it reads aGVsbG8= and reverses to 'hello' with no key

tasks.explain:
base64 reverses with no key, so it is transport encoding, never protection. The danger is real:
a credential that is merely base64'd is plaintext to anyone who decodes it — the most common
"it's encrypted" false claim an auditor meets.

tasks.instruction:
Select the real JWT header segment (`jwt.header`) and decode it live with the engine. It is
base64url — it decodes with NO key. State in your decode why a "scrambled-looking" JWT header
is plaintext to anyone.

hints.nudge: You need no key to decode a JWT header — try it; the result is readable JSON.

hints.concept: §4.1 — a JWT is a SIGNED claim, not an encrypted secret; the header is base64url

hints.reveal: Decode jwt.header — it is {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}, readable with no key

tasks.explain:
The header decodes to {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"} with no key — proof that a JWT is signed for
integrity, not encrypted for confidentiality. Anything you put in a JWT payload is readable by
anyone holding the token; the signature only stops tampering.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the "Cert · www.google.com leaf" panel and select the field that holds the in-transit
control's expiry deadline (`cert.validity.notAfter`). Read its value — this is the date past
which the in-transit claim (SC-8 / CC6.7) is dead.

hints.nudge: A certificate is only trusted inside a time window — find the END of that window.

hints.concept: §4.3 — RFC 5280 validity has notBefore and notAfter; notAfter is the deadline

hints.reveal: Select cert.validity.notAfter on the leaf; it reads 2026-08-17T08:39:10Z

tasks.explain:
The notAfter is where "encrypted in transit" goes from true to false on a calendar — an expired
cert breaks the chain even if the cipher is perfect. You just located the field an auditor
points to for the in-transit half of the claim, mapped to CC6.7 / SC-8.

tasks.instruction:
Still on the leaf, select the extension that proves this certificate is NOT allowed to sign
other certificates (`cert.basicConstraints`). Read its value.

hints.nudge: A leaf serves a website; a CA signs certificates. One extension says which this is.

hints.concept: §4.4 — RFC 5280 BasicConstraints cA distinguishes a CA cert from a leaf

hints.reveal: Select cert.basicConstraints; it reads CA:FALSE — this is a leaf, not a CA

tasks.explain:
CA:FALSE is the structural promise that this key can only authenticate a server, never mint
certificates. It is the field that, when wrong on a leaf, lets a stolen key impersonate a whole
CA — which is why the chain check (next) ends only at a cert that is genuinely a CA.

tasks.instruction:
Select the field that names which host(s) this certificate is valid for (`cert.san`). The host
you connected to must appear here, or the in-transit identity claim fails. Read its value.

hints.nudge: A cert is only valid for the names listed in one extension — find the host list.

hints.concept: §4.4 — RFC 5280 Subject Alternative Name dNSName carries the host(s) the cert covers

hints.reveal: Select cert.san; it reads DNS:www.google.com — the host the SNI must match

tasks.explain:
The SAN binds this certificate's key to a name. If the host you connected to is not covered by
the SAN, the padlock is closed but pointed at the wrong door — exactly the wrong.host break you
will diagnose later. Name-to-key binding is what a certificate IS (RFC 5280).

tasks.instruction:
Read the leaf's `cert.issuer` field — the name of the CA that signed it. To chain leaf →
intermediate → root, this issuer name must equal the next cert's subject. State the issuer.

hints.nudge: Whose name signed the leaf? Find the cert whose SUBJECT is that name — that is the next link.

hints.concept: §4.4 — each cert's issuer must equal the next cert's subject; the chain ends at a trusted root

hints.reveal: Select cert.issuer on the leaf; it reads CN=WR2 — the intermediate's subject, the next link

tasks.explain:
issuer-of-leaf == subject-of-intermediate is the predicate that draws the chain link
leaf → WR2 → GTS Root R1. A chain that does not connect (or never reaches a trusted root) is
`openssl verify` code 20 — the certificate cannot be trusted no matter how valid the leaf looks.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to the TLS 1.3 handshake builder and order the message cards into the RFC 8446
full-handshake, routing each onto Client or Server. The session opens application data only
when the order is legal; the sim runs the real §A.1 state machine.

hints.nudge: The client speaks first with its hello; the server answers before anything is encrypted; Finished closes it.

hints.concept: §4.5 — ClientHello → ServerHello → {EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished} → client Finished

hints.reveal: Order: ClientHello, ServerHello, EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, server Finished, client Finished

tasks.explain:
The order is not arbitrary — CertificateVerify (the server signing the transcript with its
private key) must follow Certificate (the public key) so the client can verify the server holds
the matching private key. The sim reaching the established state is the consequence, not a
stored "correct"; a wrong order would have raised a real alert.

tasks.instruction:
In the handshake builder, play application data BEFORE the server's Finished (the classic
break). Read the alert the sim raises and its numeric code — the protocol's real refusal, not
a "try again."

hints.nudge: The data channel is not open until the handshake finishes — the sim tells you how it objects.

hints.concept: §4.5 — RFC 8446 §6.2: an out-of-sequence message MUST terminate with unexpected_message(10)

hints.reveal: Inject application data before {Finished}; the sim raises unexpected_message(10)

tasks.explain:
unexpected_message(10) is the literal RFC 8446 §6.2 alert the state machine emits — the
handshake's integrity is structural, not advisory. The data channel does not exist until both
Finished messages are exchanged, and the protocol enforces it with a real code you can read.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to "Cert · expired.badssl.com (broken)". This real cert breaks the in-transit control
at exactly one field. Click the single field where it diverges from the clean leg and read its
value — `openssl verify` returns code 10 for this cert.

hints.nudge: Both certs are real and nearly identical — one field puts this one outside its trust window.

hints.concept: §4.6 — an expired cert is openssl verify code 10; the divergent field is notAfter

hints.reveal: On the expired panel, select cert.validity.notAfter — it reads 2015-04-12, long in the past

tasks.explain:
The notAfter of 2015-04-12 is years in the past, so the in-transit control is broken at the
calendar even though the key and chain are otherwise fine — `openssl verify` code 10
(certificate has expired). The discriminating field is the parser's computed divergence over
the real bytes, not your opinion.

tasks.instruction:
Switch to "Cert · wrong.host.badssl.com (broken)". Click the single field where this cert
fails to cover the host you connected to (`cert.san`) and read it — `openssl verify
-verify_hostname` returns code 62 for this mismatch.

hints.nudge: The padlock is valid — but for the wrong name. Read the SAN and compare it to wrong.host.badssl.com.

hints.concept: §4.6 — a SAN that does not cover the connected host is hostname mismatch, openssl code 62

hints.reveal: On the wrong-host panel, select cert.san — it covers *.badssl.com/badssl.com, NOT wrong.host.badssl.com

tasks.explain:
The SAN reads DNS:*.badssl.com, DNS:badssl.com — a single-label wildcard that does NOT cover
the three-label wrong.host.badssl.com (RFC 6125), so the cert is valid but for the wrong door:
hostname mismatch, `openssl verify` code 62. A green padlock pointed at the wrong name is the
whole point of this module's title.

tasks.instruction:
Build the re-runnable evidence verdict. Select the "Sort · SHA-256('')" card and decode it
live — confirm the empty-string digest equals the cited curriculum constant. This is a verdict
anyone can reproduce with `shasum`, the opposite of "trust the padlock."

hints.nudge: SHA-256 of the empty string is a fixed, citable constant — recompute it and compare.

hints.concept: §4.7 — a re-runnable transform output == a cited constant is evidence; the padlock is not

hints.reveal: Decode the SHA-256('') card; it is e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855

tasks.explain:
SHA-256("") = e3b0c442… is the same on every machine, forever — a verdict that reproduces is
evidence. Pair it with the negotiated TLS 1.3 / AEAD cipher line (the in-transit PASS) and the
at-rest storage-encryption setting + KMS key (CC6.1 / SC-28), and the auditor's two-part claim
is answered with bytes, not a green icon (CC6.7 / SC-8 / SC-13).

tasks.instruction:
In 5–7 sentences, for a non-technical colleague: explain the difference between hashing,
encryption, and encoding and why "it looks scrambled" is not "it is protected"; then explain
why a green padlock does not answer "is the data encrypted in transit?" and which ONE cert
field you would read to actually decide it. Use the §3 model, not jargon.

hints.nudge: The §3 model: a one-way shredder (hash), a lockbox with a key (encrypt), a different alphabet (encode).

hints.concept: §3 — The Mental Model + §4.3 the cert field that anchors the in-transit claim

fields.proves: server holds the private key for the cert's public key
